item.title: Frenchtown Advances Affordable Housing While Preserving Character
item.description:
For decades, the borough has consistently embraced its responsibility to provide diverse, accessible housing options. Rather than viewing state affordable housing mandates as a bureaucratic hurdle, Frenchtown has historically approached affordable housing as an opportunity to strengthen the community from within.

In late June, in keeping with this long-standing commitment, the borough entered into a Consent Order and Final Certificate of Compliance and Repose approved by the Superior Court of New Jersey memorializing that Frenchtown met its Fourth Round affordable housing obligation (note: the Fourth Round housing obligation refers to the 10-year statewide affordable housing cycle—2025- 2035—mandated by legislation enacted in 2024). The Certificate of Compliance is a major milestone that secures the borough’s affordable housing adherence while pioneering creative solutions tailored specifically to Frenchtown’s unique character.

item.title: Frenchtown Literary Fest Attracting Prominent Authors
item.description:
Frenchtown Bookshop’s first-ever Frenchtown Literary Festival kicked off with two events in June and continues on July 9.

The bookshop was awarded a $20,000 grant from American Express Shop Small, initially launched with a $5 million contribution to support 250 small businesses in honor of America’s 250th anniversary.

The festival, which is a series of author talks, presents “An evening with Ian Frazier” on July 9. A New Yorker essayist and humorist, he will speak in conversation with bookshop co-owner Barbara de Wilde.

item.title: Frenchtown’s 2026 Municipal Budget Approved—and Explained
item.description:
Borough Council approved the municipal budget for 2026 on May 6. In New Jersey, municipal budgets are typically adopted later in the spring because municipalities must wait for finalized figures related to state aid, county taxes and other funding obligations before accurately completing the budget process.

The borough’s 2026 budget totals $2,886,272.08; Mayor Brad Myhre says that the budget reflects a continued effort to maintain essential services while remaining mindful of the affordability challenges facing residents. The most significant driver of increased spending this year was the sharp rise in employee health care costs. Local government employers participating in the New Jersey State Health Benefits Program (NJSHBP) are facing a substantial 36.2% premium increase for Plan Year 2026, creating added financial pressure for municipalities across the state. Brad notes that, despite these rising costs, the borough’s 2026 budget maintains staffing levels and includes only modest adjustments in other spending areas.

item.title: Improvements to S. Washington Street scheduled to commence
item.description:
The South Washington Street improvement project is set to begin the first week of April.

The project includes the installation of some concrete curbs, construction of ADA curb ramps, some drainage improvements, hot mix asphalt milling, full-depth pavement repairs, full-width pavement resurfacing, traffic striping, signage and site restoration along Hawk Street (from Trenton Avenue to Front Street), Front Street (from Hawk Street to terminus), South Washington Street (from Trenton Avenue to River Road) and River Road (from South Washington Street to terminus at borough wastewater treatment plant).

item.title: New E-Bike Requirements May Cause Speed Bumps for Riders
item.description:
This summer, the state of New Jersey began implementing new e-bike rules for all residents and visitors. All e-bike owners and renters should become aware of the new requirements.

Firstly, what is an e-bike? The law defines “e-bike” as both low-speed electric bicycles with a motor that only provides assistance while pedaling up to 20 miles per hour (mph) as well as motorized bicycles equipped with either a helper motor or an electric motor.

item.title: Frenchtown Mourns the Loss of Rick Epstein, Historian, Author and Founder of _The Sun_
item.description:
It is with the heaviest hearts that the editorial team of The Frenchtown Sun shares the loss of one of our founders, Rick Epstein.

The Frenchtown Sun was born out of a desire for more local news and Rick joined early conversations to develop our current newsletter iteration. He named The Sun and provided editorial content and suggestions up through our June issue, shortly before his passing.

The only one of us with editorial experience—and extensive experience at that—Rick was our guiding light. He would (very gently, as was Rick’s way) chide us for “spinach” content—pieces that lacked a human-interest element or intriguing hook. At every editorial discussion, we find ourselves asking, “What Would Rick Do?” His wisdom and guidance continue to provide support for The Sun.

item.title: Madison Rose Finery Opens on Bridge St.
item.description:
Madison Rose Finery is the new boutique at 22 Bridge St., a space formerly occupied by the Sublime gift shop.

Gemologist and designer Madison Rose Whitman offers fine antique and estate jewelry, responsibly sourced gemstones, and an ever-evolving collection of handmade art and gifts. The shop provides a full range of jewelry services, including custom design, repair and restoration, appraisals, estate buying, consignment, expert consultations, and rare object sourcing.

“The boutique blends expertise, artistry, and storytelling, offering both locals and visitors a place to find meaningful gifts, celebrate milestones, or simply wander and be inspired,” says Madison Rose. “Drawing on a deep passion for gemology, natural history, and the wonder of discovery, the showroom is a quietly enchanting space where curious objects blur the line between adornment and artifact.”

item.title: Operation Blue Angel will help residents during medical emergencies
item.description:
The Frenchtown Police Department, in partnership with the Age-Friendly Frenchtown Initiative, now offers Operation Blue Angel, a voluntary program designed to assist Frenchtown Borough residents who are at risk of a medical or life-threatening emergency and may be home alone, unable to get to the front door to open it for help.

The program allows first responders to enter a resident’s home without unnecessary delays or potential damage to windows or doors when someone is unable to answer the door.

item.title: Worst Tick Season in a Decade is Predicted
item.description:
Experts are warning that 2026 is turning out to be the worst tick season in 9 years, and New Jersey is right in the thick of it. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) reports that early-spring emergency room visits for tick bites have reached their highest levels since 2017.

To stay safe this season, Frenchtown residents should be “tick-aware” and follow these essential precautions:

  • Wear light-colored clothing so ticks are easier to spot and tuck your pants into your socks.
  • Thoroughly check yourself, your children, and your pets upon coming indoors.
  • Stay on the path: Keep children and pets from running into underbrush along walking trails.
  • Use repellent: The CDC recommends using repellents registered with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency containing DEET, picaridin, IR3535, Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus (OLE), para-menthane-diol (PMD) or 2-undecanone. For more information, see: https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/prevention/index.html.

To learn more about ticks and watch a step-by-step video on how to properly remove them, visit https://extension.rutgers.edu/tick. Additionally, scientists at the Rutgers NJ Ticks 4 Science program are asking residents to send in ticks they encounter which will be used to create a real-time tick tracking map. To learn how to mail in a tick, visit ticks.rutgers.edu.

item.title: Environmental Commission wants to control invasive vines with beetles
item.description:
When you see leaves that look like this, you’re looking at trouble.

As the soil warms up this spring, seedlings of the invasive and terribly aggressive Mile-a-Minute vine (Persicaria perfoliata) will sprout. Also known as devil’s tail, giant climbing tearthumb, and Asiatic tearthumb, this vine grows extremely rapidly and can take over gardens and woodlands, overgrowing shrubs, trees and outdoor furniture and buildings.

Single plants can easily grow up to 25-feet-long or more in a single season. The almost perfectly triangular blue-green leaves are easy to identify, and the entire plant is armed with tiny, hooked barbs that will catch on clothing and skin.

item.title: Frenchtown Elementary School Leadership
item.description: KATE NUGENT has served on the Frenchtown Board of Education for 20 years, and as president for most of that time. Frenchtown has a seven-member elected board whose job is to ensure that the school is well run. Their duties include setting district policies and goals, overseeing the budget, hiring and evaluating administrators, and serving as the communications link between the community and the school. As president, Kate is the primary spokesperson for the board. She ensures that meetings are conducted efficiently and works closely with the superintendent to discuss long-range plans. The responsibilities of the president are different from other board members, but her authority is not. She still only has one vote.

item.title: Letter from the editor
item.description:
I moved to Frenchtown in the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic. What I thought would be the beginnings of a charming life in a colorful small town was instead full of distance and isolation. Despite this bleak beginning, Frenchtown has demonstrated again and again over the last six years that we are a community of generous support, value and friendship.

Whether it’s chatting with neighbors on my front porch, waving to visitors on the path during a midday run or bumping into friends old and new during Riverfest, our little hamlet on the river has become my most treasured place: my home.

item.title: Planning Board Considering Tightening Data Center Regulations
item.description:
Data centers and their impact on communities have been featured prominently in the news across the country. On May 27, Gov. Mikie Sherrill announced a comprehensive statewide plan to address the impact of data centers on local communities.

The Frenchtown Planning Board will be considering the need for any changes to the borough ordinance regarding data centers. The board will study ordinances from other small municipalities, looking into the definitions of data centers (large and small). The board aims to advise council of any need to change the borough land use ordinance later this year.

item.title: Updates from Borough Council
item.description:
At its monthly meeting on July 1, Borough Council discussed the installation of flashing beacons at the Kingwood Ave. crosswalk in July, and a $200,000 grant in the recently approved New Jersey state budget to support improvements to the interior of Borough Hall. Additionally, the Council:

  • Authorized Collier’s Engineering to issue a Request for Proposal for a contractor to install a half-pipe skateboard ramp at Borough Park and to undertake necessary improvements at Borough Park to facilitate installation of the ramp. The expectation is that the equipment will be installed by the end of 2026; a rendering of the ramp is below. Several Frenchtown residents attended the meeting and offered their appreciation for the work of the Council to advance the installation of the skateboard ramp using county grant funds.
  • Approved several events sponsored by the Frenchtown Business and Professional Association including Riverfest on September 6, the Witches Dance and Zombie Crawl on October 24 and Santa on the River on December 6. More information about these events can be found on the FBPA website: lovefrenchtown.org/. Additionally, the Council approved the Sojourn Stopover of the Lenape Nation of Pennsylvania at Sunbeam Lenape Park on August 9.
  • Appointed Neil Palmer to the borough’s Environmental Commission. Resident Barbara Bristow serves as Acting Chair of the Commission. Other members include: Kyle Johnson, Pete Palac, Chris Szeplaki and Armin Zomorodi; Ted Brandston serves as the Planning Board’s liaison to the Commission. The Council also had a first reading on an ordinance that would establish additional alternate members to the Environmental Commission; the draft ordinance will have its second and final reading at the Council’s August meeting.
  • Approved a grant application to the New Jersey Department of Transportation for funds to address road resurfacing, road draining, and pavement improvements on roads on Third, Fourth and Fifth Streets.
  • Appointed Patrick Keelen to the borough’s Shade Tree Commission. Other members of the Shade Tree Commission include chair Geoff Stanly, Mark Loos, Melissa Allen and John Mizin.
  • Authorized a Fire/EMS grant application towards the purchase of an ambulance by the Milford-Holland Rescue Squad which serves Frenchtown.
  • Had a first reading of an ordinance that would appropriate approximately $62,000 from the borough’s Capital Improvement Fund for an upfit of a currently-owned police department vehicle to make it “patrol ready,” and renovations for Borough Hall. The renovation funds were requested prior to the $200,000 appropriation in the state budget and can be returned if not needed.

item.title: Updates from Borough Council
item.description:
At its monthly meeting on August 5, Borough Council conducted the following items of business:

  • approved an ordinance to revise the Borough Code to allow the Environmental Commission to have two alternative positions;
  • approved a capital ordinance for various borough improvements, including costs to upfit a vehicle currently owned by the borough to make it “patrol ready” for the Police Department, a new vehicle for day-to-day operational use and renovations to Borough Hall;
  • authorized the preparation and submission of grant applications to the Large Foundation of Flemington, NJ and the Astle-Alpaugh Foundation to fund the operations of Age Friendly Frenchtown;
  • received several bids for the Pump Station and Department of Public Works (DPW) facility generator project. Power and Prestige Inc. in Newton, NJ will be awarded the contract;
  • appointed Carole Pepe as a part-time, as needed, library assistant and authorized the acceptance of a student volunteer to perform volunteer services for the borough;
  • acknowledged that the DPW erected a new flagpole outside Borough Hall with financial support from the Fargo Family Foundation;
  • shared that the town administrator and borough engineer had a pre-construction meeting with Comcast. Comcast will be installing three structures around the borough, in the right of way on Hawk St., Maple Ave. and Railroad Ave. to bring fiber connectivity to Frenchtown;
  • announced that street sweeping is tentatively scheduled for September 1 from 7 a.m. – 9 a.m. Parking will be restricted briefly on Race St. and Bridge St. No vehicles need to be moved in the residential areas;
  • announced that tax bills are now available online although paper copies are also available at Borough Hall if you have not received your mailed copy. The State of New Jersey was late in providing the borough approval, so tax bills were sent out late. There will be an extension until September 4;
  • shared two items from the Police Department: 1) in late July, a large group of motorcyclists rode into town, one individual was arrested and his vehicle was impounded and 2) there was a dog bite incident off the river path near the Harrison Square apartment complex; the dog was leashed and the person received proper medical attention on the scene.

item.title: Meet Lions Club President Albert Giarretta
item.description:
ALBERT GIARRETTA has served as a member of the Frenchtown Lions Club for 30 years and as its president for the past four.

Celebrating its 90th anniversary in 2026, the club remains a vital non-profit service organization in the greater Frenchtown area. The Lions raise funds to provide holiday gifts for families in need, host the annual Easter Egg Hunt and present community service awards to 8th grade and graduating high school seniors. Additionally, the local chapter supports the International Lions Club and raises funds to help prevent eye diseases.

item.title: Meet the Frenchtown Police Department
item.description:
Each of Frenchtown’s police officers is devoted to a community‑centered style of policing, focusing on being approachable, engaged, and connected with the people he serves. They value the close connections that define small-town policing and take pride in being part of a department whose daily work is guided by compassion for our residents.

From left to right: Ptl. Kevin Coletta, Ptl. David Lugo, and Sgt. Erik Eccles

item.title: Meet your mayor
item.description:
BRAD MYHRE was born and raised in Frenchtown Borough and has served as mayor since 2015.

During his tenure, Myhre has helped lead several important infrastructure improvements and redevelopment initiatives that have strengthened the community and supported the borough’s continued growth. In addition to his work in local government, Myhre is a dedicated fan of the New York Giants and Penn State Nittany Lions football, and enjoys spending time with friends, testing his knowledge during trivia nights at Wild Fern Brewery.

item.title: Shade Structure Will Provide Respite from Sun at Kingwood Dog Park
item.description:
The Kingwood Dog Park, an off-leash dog area located at 178 Horseshoe Bend Rd. in Horseshoe Bend Park, will have a shade structure erected for dogs and their human companions to enjoy a break from the sun in the coming months.

The Kingwood Township Parks & Recreation Board committed $800 to the structure, along with promising to handle the permitting and installation. Generous local residents raised an additional $1,500 to ensure there is enough funding for the project.

item.title: Meet Del Val BOE Rep Tom Loughlin
item.description: TOM LOUGHLIN has represented Frenchtown on the Delaware Valley Regional High School (Del Val) Board of Education (BOE) since January 2024. Located on Senator Stout Rd. in Frenchtown, Del Val serves Alexandria, Frenchtown, Holland, Kingwood and Milford. The nine-member, publicly elected BOE oversees the school’s budget, curriculum, policies and personnel decisions. Current challenges facing Del Val include an ever-challenging budget, artificial intelligence, cell phone use and declining enrollment. The BOE is focused on maintaining academic and holistic student excellence while keeping strict oversight of the budget.

item.title: Meet FBPA President Morgan Taylor
item.description:
MORGAN TAYLOR is the President of the Frenchtown Business & Professional Association, a position that she has held for more than 3 years.

The FBPA, also known as Love Frenchtown, is a volunteer run, member-supported, non-profit organization dedicated to supporting local business and enriching the Frenchtown community. Mobilizing through town events, downtown beautification efforts, strong relationships with other community interest groups and expressing a voice in local government, the FBPA is an active part of civic life in the borough.

item.title: Meet your Borough Council
item.description:
MICHELE LIEBTAG is President of the Frenchtown Borough Council and Commissioner, overseeing the police and fire departments. She has been a borough resident since 2003. Michele is also the vice chair of the Hunterdon County Democratic Committee and the political and education director for CWA Local 1036.

KATHLEEN BERNHARDT was elected to the council in 2025. She is the council liaison to the Frenchtown Library and the Department of Public Works. Bernhardt has been a resident of Hunterdon County for more than 30 years, living in Frenchtown since 2018. A former Frenchtown business owner (The Junto Emporium), Bernhardt can now be found most evenings working as hostess at FiNNBAR.

item.title: Meet your Borough staff
item.description: CHRISTOPHER (CHRIS) DEWIRE is Frenchtown’s borough administrator and director of public safety. He was hired in March 2025, and he currently manages daily operations of all borough departments. He is the primary liaison between staff, the mayor, and the Borough Council. A lifelong resident of Hunterdon County, Chris retired from the Readington Township Police Department in 2024 as a lieutenant and officer-in-charge. He is a former member of the Hunterdon County SWAT team and was a mobile intensive care paramedic at Hunterdon Medical Center for 25 years. Chris has two grown children and is proud to serve the Frenchtown community. Chris’ email is: director@frenchtownboro.gov.

item.title: Much-anticipated improvements coming to Harrison Street sidewalks
item.description:
After more than a year of coordination with property owners along Harrison Street, all required access agreements have been secured, clearing the way for long-awaited sidewalk improvements. The project will include resetting existing pavers to eliminate tripping hazards and upgrading non-compliant ADA ramps to improve accessibility for all residents.

The Borough of Frenchtown was awarded a 2016 Safe Routes to School grant totaling $472,000 through the North Jersey Transportation Planning Authority to support this effort. While these grants typically move from award to construction within five to seven years, this project faced additional delays due to stringent federal requirements, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the time-intensive process of securing access agreements from all adjacent property owners.

item.title: These River Rats Go the Distance
item.description:
If you spot a group of smiling runners along the river path, you are likely encountering the River Rats Running Club.

Formed 7 years ago, the club welcomes novice and experienced runners from the Delaware River region—from Lambertville/New Hope to Riegelsville and beyond. Founded by William Semon and run by a dedicated Board of Directors, the club also recently achieved official nonprofit status to promote and support safe and organized physical fitness in the region.

item.title: Frenchtown is getting “age-friendlier”
item.description:
In March 2025, Frenchtown received a $70,000 grant from the state Department of Human Services to build community partnerships, assess the needs of our older residents, and create an “age-friendly” action plan. That plan is expected to be on the agenda at the June 4 Borough Council meeting.

The age-friendly effort is led by AARP nationally to help communities become more livable for the elderly. Frenchtown is already considered age-friendly, scoring 61 on AARP’s national Livability Index. The nationwide average score was 50. But we could be even friendlier.
More than 45% of households in Frenchtown include at least one person age 60 or older; the median income of residents age 65+ is $67,596 as compared to Hunterdon’s average of $90,843 for the same age group.

item.title: Hunterdon to Celebrate 250th with Symphony Concert and Fireworks
item.description:
Hunterdon County will celebrate the nation’s 250th birthday on Wednesday, July 8, 7-10:30 p.m. at Deer Path Park in Flemington. The party will include live music from the Hunterdon Symphony, what’s billed as the largest display of fireworks Hunterdon has ever seen, food trucks and a dramatic reading of the Declaration of Independence by Revolutionary War by a re-enactor portraying Revolutionary War hero Ned Hector.

This event is free and open to the public. Organizers recommend arriving early to secure the best spots, bringing a blanket and/or lawn chairs, and wearing red, white and blue. If you have questions, contact 300info@co.hunterdon.nj.us.

item.title: Environmental Commission Hosts “Weevilpalooza” for all ages on July 3
item.description:
The Frenchtown Environmental Commission will host Weevilpalooza on Friday, July 3 at 5:30 p.m. in the Frenchtown Preserve.

This is a family-friendly opportunity to learn about biological control of invasive species. Join commission members to release 1,000 weevils (Rhinoncomimus latipes) directly onto patches of the Mile-A-Minute vine (Persicaria perfoliata), an aggressive invasive plant that smothers native vegetation by blocking sunlight.

A biological control agent, these weevils have been thoroughly researched and have successfully managed the Mile-A-Minute vine since 2004. The weevil only feeds on the vine, weakening the plants and reducing their ability to produce seed and spread. Decreasing the seed production is the key to controlling it. Weevils were purchased from the state by a grant secured by the Environmental Commission.

item.title: Planning Board reviewing master plan
item.description:
The Frenchtown Planning Board has just begun a five-year review of the most recent master plan re-examination report (dated 2021).

What is a master plan? It is a blueprint for a municipality, outlining a vision for the future of the borough consisting of balanced economic, social, physical, environmental, and fiscal planning. While not a set of laws or regulations, a master plan provides guidance to the borough when making land use, zoning, and capital investment decisions.

item.title: Frenchtown and Kingwood Methodist Churches to Merge and Become Open Door
item.description:
Frenchtown and Kingwood United Methodist Churches will soon become the Open Door United Methodist Church, meeting at the Frenchtown church at 16 Third Street. Services will be on Sundays at 9 a.m. starting July 5 and will include a monthly dinner church service each month on third Sundays at 5 p.m.

Kingwood UMC is the oldest Methodist church in Hunterdon, and its site on Route 519 in southern Kingwood has hosted a church since the 1780s. At one time, the Kingwood church held several roast beef dinners a year that funded organizations such as rescue and fire squads, the Flemington Food Pantry, an animal rescue organization and more. In addition, Kingwood UMC has awarded over $50,000 in scholarships to Del Val High School students since 2019. Kingwood’s philanthropic spirit will be united with Frenchtown’s.

item.title: Spotlight: Frenchtown Fire Department
item.description:
Residents may have seen the Frenchtown Fire Department (FFD) supporting members of the community throughout the borough, including, most recently, during the July storm that caused significant tree damage and power outages in the area.

The FFD typically responds to 125-150 calls each year and there are currently 12 volunteers on the FFD roster.

Firefighting operations in the borough operate under a model that is intended to separate emergency operations from business or fundraising administration. Under this model, the FFD chief manages all on-scene emergency operations, training protocols, apparatus readiness and equipment procurement. The Union Fire Company, an independent, non-profit organization, manages facilities, organizational bylaws, finances and membership. Additionally, Frenchtown participates in a county-wide mutual aid agreement that includes municipal fire departments throughout Hunterdon and Bucks Counties. This agreement ensures a reciprocal system where Frenchtown and neighboring departments automatically dispatch extra firefighters, specialized equipment and emergency personnel to support one another whenever required.

item.title: FES and DVRHS 2026 Budget Overview
item.description:
In 2025, approximately 38% of Frenchtown’s property taxes funded the borough’s contribution to Frenchtown Elementary School (FES) and more than 23% went to Delaware Valley Regional High School (DVRHS) (see figure at left). While figures are not yet available for 2026, the two schools’ budgets are now finalized.

In New Jersey, public school districts cannot raise their property tax levy by more than 2% over the previous year without having available Statutory Spending Growth Limitation Adjustments or through voter approval.

item.title: Former ArtYard visiting artist to give Frenchtown’s “Jane Doe” a headstone

On Oct. 26, 1991, the body of a teenage girl was found by hunters in Warren County just off Interstate 80 not far from the Delaware River. Due to decomposition, the authorities could not determine the cause of her death, but it was declared a homicide.

Over the past eight months, the borough has undertaken an “Age-Friendly” planning process, which will culminate with Borough Council adopting an Age-Friendly Action Plan this June. The Action Plan will summarize challenges and opportunities to promoting Age-Friendliness in the borough and outline priority actions moving forward as part of its Age-Friendly initiative.

item.title: Borough considering parking meters
item.description:
Turnover of parking spaces in downtown Frenchtown continues to be a significant challenge, particularly as warmer weather brings an increase in visitors. On weekends, many people park in municipal lots to access the D&R Canal Path, often leaving their vehicles for the entire day without visiting local businesses. This limits availability for customers who are looking to shop, dine, and support the downtown.

To address this issue, the borough is actively discussing the potential implementation of parking meters—an approach successfully used in many comparable river towns—to encourage greater turnover of parking spaces.

item.title: Early Freeze Harms Local Orchards, Including Nagy’s Peaches
item.description:
Northern Red Oak (Quercus rubra) leaves the day after the freeze on April 22.

It seems like a long time ago, but back on April 21 of this year, Frenchtown experienced a record-breaking hard freeze (as low as 23°F) that has had some long-term consequences for farms, trees and wildlife in our area.

Many plants, including mature hardwood trees, had already leafed out and the new leaves simply froze in place. Oak trees, hackberries, and others had all or most of their young leaves completely frozen and killed. Even young acorns, hackberry “berries,” maple seeds, and many other tree and shrub fruits (critical for wildlife) were frozen and killed. Countless flowering trees, from apple, peach and cherry trees at local farms, to flowering dogwoods and redbuds in yards and woodlands, had their flowers or young fruits frozen and killed. Even blueberries and strawberry crops were hard hit.

item.title: A Friendly Greeting Makes a Difference
item.description: Several long-time Frenchtown residents have noticed a shift: more people are skipping a “hello” when encountering their neighbors, even when someone else starts the greeting. These locals miss that old-school friendliness, noting that Frenchtown has always been a community where people look out for one another. Research shows that a simple greeting is more than just good manners—it makes people feel seen and helps neighbors feel connected. By speaking up, you break the ice and demonstrate a more welcoming community. Next time you’re out on the path, consider a hearty “hello!” You’ll be glad you did.

item.title: You Won’t Be Able to Buy These Plants
item.description: On January 20th, the New Jersey Invasive Species Management Act (NJISMA) was signed into law after more than 20 years of planning and discussion among scientists, environmental organizations, the NJ nursery industry, land managers and other stakeholders. This new act lists 30 invasive plant species (currently) that are now illegal to propagate, import/export, sell, or advertise—in other words, no one will be able to buy and plant these species in NJ anymore.

item.title: In Memoriam: Rick Epstein
item.description:
Rick Epstein, 75, of Frenchtown died at home on July 20.

Born in Syracuse, NY, Rick was raised in Lawrence Township and graduated from Lawrence High School in 1969 and from Syracuse University in 1973 with a bachelor’s degree in journalism.

He held his dream job as editor of the Delaware Valley News in Frenchtown from 1977-1984. After becoming a parent, he worked as a managing editor at the Somerset Messenger-Gazette in Somerville, the Green Brook-North Plainfield Journal and the Highland Park Herald. He spent six years as a copy editor at the Central New Jersey Home News before coming to the Hunterdon County Democrat in 1995 where he was managing editor for many years. Rick contributed reporting and photography through 2015. Instead of entering retirement, Rick worked as a full-time library aide at Delaware Valley Regional High School from 2016-2025, where he also gave presentations to the journalism and history students, and photographed school activities for his write-ups on the school’s social media channels.

item.title: Frenchtown then & now
item.description: Race Street is in better shape nowadays, and current parental “best practices” preclude parking babies on it. Note the National Hotel in the background on the right. The PRINTING sign marks the site of William Sipes’ shop and office of his Frenchtown Star newspaper, and indicates the photo was taken no earlier than 1879 and sometime before 1885, when Sipes’ operation had moved to the other side of Race Street. The buildings on the left were among the five demolished in 1954 and replaced by the yellow-brick building that wraps around the inside corner of Bridge and Race. The redeveloper was Edward Flecker, who did the plumbing for Hunterdon Medical Center and Del Val High School. The old photo is artificially colorized and maybe doesn’t do justice to the carpet the baby is sitting on. —Rick Epstein

item.title: Frenchtown then & now
item.description: The Barn Theatre was built in 1939 between upper Eleventh and Twelfth Streets. It had 477 comfortable seats and a knotty-pine foyer. Its first show was Stagecoach, starring John Wayne. The photo on the left was taken in 1941. Nelverna Bellis, manager from the 1940s into the 1970s, was very strict. No feet on the upholstery, and young lovers found a chilly climate that had nothing to do with the air conditioning. It is said that Nelverna would slap the hands of hand-holders, although that’s hard to believe. In 1989 it showed its last film, When Harry Met Sally, starring Meg Ryan and Billy Crystal. Proprietor Richard Nathan, said that the Barn had been losing money ever since the 1982 opening of Cinema Plaza, a multi-screen theater near Flemington. —Rick Epstein

item.title: What WWII Troops Told the Principal
item.description:
In the cellar of the Frenchtown School, there are many things, including 75 cardboard banker’s boxes. Most of them are filled with boring stuff like old invoices, audit reports, school-board meeting agendas and minutes, and personnel and student records.

But one of them contains a thick folder full of letters and postcards received by Principal Bert Light during World War II. He was in charge of the K-12 school in 1931-59, and was something of a father figure. He’d been an Army officer in World War I. So, some of his alumni, in uniform, wrote home to him.

item.title: Frenchtown then & now
item.description: THE ODD FELLOWS BUILDING at 17-19 Bridge Street is 47 feet tall, making it Frenchtown’s tallest. Completed in 1897, it was built for the Independent Order of Odd Fellows, Frenchtown’s most prestigious and affluent lodge. The lodge brothers, who were dedicated to doing good deeds, met on the third story. When the picture (below, left) was taken circa 1930, the lodge was still going strong. In the 2026 photo (below, right), the building is missing its next-door neighbor. Over the years, that brick residence was the home of Bridge Street merchants Hugh Warford (b. 1826-d.1887), Charles N. Reading (1854-1919), and Samuel Frenchtown then & now O. Eddy (1864-1934). It was saved from the Great Frenchtown Fire of 1878 by men with ladders, buckets, and strips of wet carpet. But in 1962 Wilbur Stout of Pennington bought it and let it decay, finally demolishing it in 1972. —Rick Epstein

item.title: Frenchtown then & now
item.description: The Hummer Building, as some of the old-timers call it, is on the left. The western half of it was built by druggist and liniment manufacturer Albert Williams right after the Great Fire of 1878 on the ashes of his former building. The original tenant on the corner was George W. Hummer’s furniture and undertaking business. Williams’ pharmacy was next door. Lorenzo Kerr put up the other half in 1881. His original tenant was DeWitt C. Dalrymple’s store, whose wares included corsets, men’s straw hats, lace curtains, feathers, and parasols. (Ten years later, Mr. Dalrymple was yardmaster of a Hoboken railyard and was run over by a train). The current owner is Jill Kearney, who also owns FiNNBAR. Although she is the founder and executive director of ArtYard, these are her personal holdings. —Rick Epstein

item.title: History Spotlight: The Fargo Family Foundation
item.description: For over a century, the Fargo family name has been deeply rooted in Frenchtown. As chronicled in Rick Epstein’s local histories, Frenchtown and More Frenchtown, the family’s legacy in the borough began with patriarch Clarence B. Fargo. Professionally, Clarence operated a printing and publishing bus-iness in Frenchtown, running a mail-order flower-seed and bulb business out of a commercial building on Bridge Street, alongside his work documenting local history. Beyond his business ventures, Clarence was an active community member who engaged deeply with the local area, eventually authoring the foundational History of Frenchtown in 1933.
